name: Editorial
basis: magazine-cover layout: masthead fitting, legibility gradients, decorative barcode (how)

lumenary.blurb: A magazine cover: masthead, cover lines, issue line and a barcode.

facts.bestOn: Portraits and strong single subjects, portrait orientation

why: A magazine cover is a small problem in hierarchy: one image, one masthead, and a few short lines that must be readable over anything. This treatment solves it the way a layout program would. It darkens the top and bottom so white type stays legible, stretches the masthead to the exact page width, and wraps the headline to fit.
how: Fill the page with the photograph, optionally in monochrome or a warm sepia tone computed in code.
Add dark gradients at the top and bottom so type stays readable.
Measure the masthead and scale it so it spans the page.
Wrap the headline on spaces, shrinking the type by ten percent until it fits in three lines.
Place the issue line, the cover lines and a decorative barcode.
history: Illustrated magazine covers developed through the late nineteenth century, and by the 1920s titles such as Time and Vogue had settled on the formula of a strong image under a recognisable masthead. The barcode on covers came later: the first product scanned with a barcode was a pack of chewing gum in 1974. The barcode here is only for decoration, since its bar widths are random.
uses: “Cover story” posts for birthdays and milestones
terms: The title of a magazine at the top of its cover.
The short teasers printed around the main image.
Filling each line with as many words as fit, then starting a new line.
paragraphs: The cover is built like a layout program would build it. The photograph fills the page; for the monochrome and warm options its pixels are first converted in code (a weighted grey with extra contrast, or a mix of the original and a sepia colour matrix), so the result does not depend on browser filters. Dark gradients at the top and bottom keep the white type readable whatever the picture is.

The masthead is measured and scaled so that it spans exactly the width of the page. The headline is wrapped greedily on spaces; if it needs more than three lines the type shrinks by 10% until it fits. The barcode is a run of bars with random widths from a fixed seed, so it is the same every time.

equations.note: The sepia colour matrix. The warm option blends 45% of it with the original colour.
Masthead size s: w₁₀₀ is the measured width of the word at size 100, and u is one percent of the shorter side.

presets.text: Monochrome with a quiet accent is the serious, fashion-magazine look.
Warm tone and a new headline make a travel cover.
Strip it back to the masthead and photograph only.
